title: How to Add Sheet Music to Google Docs and Slides (Write, Play and Edit Scores)
ex: Google Docs and Slides have no built-in music notation. Three ways to add sheet music: special characters, a picture of a score, or an add-on that writes, plays and re-edits scores.
alt: A melody with chord names inserted on a Google Slides slide, with the Music Notation sidebar open
eyealt: Add sheet music to Google Docs and Slides
html:
Short answer: Google Docs and Google Slides have no built-in way to write sheet music. You can type a few music symbols from Insert → Special characters, or paste a picture of a score made in another program. To write a real score inside the document, use an add-on. Music Notation for Docs & Slides (made by us) lets you type the music as plain text, hear it, and insert it as a sharp picture that you can open and edit again later.

Written: November 2026, Google Docs and Google Slides in Chrome.

Which situation are you in?

  • One or two symbols in a sentence (♩ ♪ ♫ ♭ ♯): Method 1.
  • You already have the score in MuseScore, Noteflight or a PDF: Method 2.
  • You want to write and change the score inside Docs or Slides (a worksheet, a lesson, a song sheet): Method 3.

Compare the ways

Method 1: Type music symbols

  1. In Google Docs, click where the symbol should go.
  2. Choose Insert → Special characters.
  3. Type music in the search box, or draw the symbol, and click the one you want.

This is fine for a note in running text ("play the ♩ = 100 section"). It cannot draw a staff, a melody or chords. In Google Slides, copy the symbol from a Doc, or type it with your computer's symbol picker (Win + . on Windows, Ctrl + Cmd + Space on a Mac).

Method 2: Insert a picture of a score

  1. Write the music in your notation program and export it as PNG (or take a screenshot of the part you need).
  2. In Docs or Slides, choose Insert → Image → Upload from computer.
  3. Resize it. In Docs, set Image options → Wrap text → In line so it moves with the text.

It looks right, but the picture is fixed. To change one note, you go back to the other program, export again and replace the image. Export at a large size so it does not blur when printed.

Method 3: Write the score in the sidebar (add-on)

Music Notation for Docs & Slides is an add-on made by us, Daily Picks. You type the music in ABC notation, a simple text format (for example C D E F | G2 G2 |). The score is drawn as you type, you can press Play to hear it, and Insert score puts it in the document or on the slide.

  1. Install Music Notation from the Google Workspace Marketplace.
  2. Open a document (click where the score should go) or a presentation.
  3. Choose Extensions → Music Notation for Docs & Slides → Open Music Notation.
  4. Pick a starter (melody with chords, song with lyrics, scale, note-naming worksheet, piano) or type your own, then press Insert score.
  5. To change it later, click the score once, press Edit the selected score…, change the music and press Update. It stays in the same place and at the same width.

What you can write: notes, rests, repeats, ties and slurs, triplets, key and time signatures, tempo, chord names above the staff, lyrics under the notes, and two or more staves for piano. Scores are inserted at twice the screen resolution on a white background, so they print sharply.

The add-on uses only the file you have open, and your music is not sent anywhere. The music is kept in the picture's alt text inside your file, which is how it can be opened again. The free version inserts up to 5 scores per file, with no watermark, and editing is always free. Paid sets are one-time purchases ($9 each): transposing, guitar and bass tabs and drums, and large PNG/SVG/MIDI downloads with practice mode. Everything is $24 one-time; an optional subscription adds a score library and a quiz maker for teachers. Details are on the Music Notation product page.

Pitfalls

  • Pictures of scores cannot be searched or edited. If you might change the music, keep the source (your notation file, or ABC text) with the document.
  • Small exports blur on paper. Export at two or three times the size you need and shrink it in the document.
  • Pasted scores move around in Docs. Use In line wrapping so the score stays with the paragraph above it.

FAQ

Can I write sheet music directly in Google Docs? Not with the built-in tools. Docs has music symbols in Special characters but no staff. An add-on can draw the score and insert it.

Can I edit the score after inserting it? A pasted picture, no. A score inserted with Music Notation, yes: select it and press Edit the selected score….

Does it work in Google Slides? Yes. In Slides the score goes in the middle of the current slide, and you can move and resize it like any picture.

What is ABC notation? A plain-text way to write music that has been used for decades for folk tunes. Letters are notes, numbers are lengths and | is a bar line. The add-on's starters show the common patterns.

title: How to Add Events from Google Sheets to Google Calendar (CSV Import or Add-on)
ex: Turn a schedule in Google Sheets into Google Calendar events: the CSV import and its pitfalls (no undo, duplicates), a script, and an add-on that reads your table with a preview and undo.
eyealt: Add events from Google Sheets to Google Calendar
html:
Short answer: Google Calendar can import a CSV file. Save the sheet as CSV with English headers (Subject, Start Date, Start Time, End Date, End Time and so on), then use Settings → Import & export → Import. It works, but the headers and date format must match exactly, nothing is shown before the events are added, and there is no undo. For a schedule you update again and again, an add-on such as Calendar Import for Google Sheets (made by us) reads the table as it is, shows a preview, skips rows already added and can undo the last import.

Written: November 2026, Google Sheets and Google Calendar in Chrome.

Which situation are you in?

  • A one-off list in a format you can change: the CSV import is enough (Method 1).
  • You add events from a sheet often and know a little code: Method 2.
  • A class timetable, shift table or deadline list that keeps changing: Method 3.

Compare the ways

Method 1: Import a CSV file

  1. Arrange the sheet so row 1 has these English headers: Subject, Start Date, Start Time, End Date, End Time, All Day Event, Description, Location. Only Subject and Start Date are required.
  2. Write dates like 11/30/2026 and times like 10:00 AM, the format in Google's own example.
  3. Choose File → Download → Comma-separated values (.csv).
  4. In Google Calendar on a computer, click the gear → Settings → Import & export, choose the file, choose the calendar, and click Import.

Things to know before you import:

  • There is no undo. If something is wrong you delete the events one by one. A safer habit: create a new calendar for the import first. If it goes wrong, delete that calendar and everything in it goes too.
  • Importing again adds everything again. Calendar does not know which rows it already has.
  • Guests are not imported and repeating events arrive as separate one-time events (Google's help page says so).

Method 2: Write a short Apps Script

In the sheet, Extensions → Apps Script lets you write code that calls CalendarApp.getDefaultCalendar().createEvent(title, start, end) for each row. It is flexible, but you handle date parsing, time zones, duplicates and mistakes yourself, and the script asks for access to your calendar the first time it runs.

Method 3: Import the table as it is (add-on)

Calendar Import for Google Sheets is an add-on made by us, Daily Picks. It reads the table you already have: it guesses the columns from your headers (Title, Date, Start time, End time, Location, Description and many more), and reads dates such as 2026-11-07, 11/7, Nov 7, 2026 or 7 Nov 2026, and times such as 9:30 AM, 3pm, 15:00 or a range like 9:00-17:30 in one cell.

  1. Install Calendar Import from the Google Workspace Marketplace.
  2. Open the sheet (header row, one event per row) and click inside the table.
  3. Choose Extensions → Calendar Import for Google Sheets → Import to Calendar.
  4. Check the columns, choose the calendar, and press Check what will be added. It lists how many events will be added and every row it cannot read, with the reason.
  5. Press Add to Calendar. If something is wrong, press Undo (twice to confirm).

Times go to the calendar exactly as written, with a time zone, so 9:00 in the sheet is 9:00 in the calendar, across daylight-saving changes too. Night shifts such as 22:00–6:00 end the next day. A guests column is never used, so no invitations are sent. Press the button again after adding new rows and the rows already in the calendar are skipped.

The add-on reads only the sheet you have open and never writes to it. It changes your calendar only when you press a button. The free version adds up to 20 events per import (press again for the rest) and includes the preview, duplicate skipping and undo. The paid version (a one-time $19, no subscription) removes the limit, updates only the rows that changed, and sets the calendar, color and reminder per row. Details are on the Calendar Import product page.

Pitfalls

  • Events at the wrong hour: the CSV import uses the calendar's time zone. If the sheet was written for another time zone, the times shift. Check the time zone in Calendar settings before importing.
  • Dates read the wrong way round: 03/04/2026 can be March 4 or April 3. In a CSV for Calendar, use month/day/year as in Google's example.
  • A blank row ends the table for most tools, including ours. Remove blank rows or select the whole range first.

FAQ

Can Google Sheets add events to Google Calendar automatically? Not with a built-in button. Use the CSV import, a script, or an add-on.

How do I undo a CSV import in Google Calendar? There is no undo. Delete the events by hand, or, if you imported into a separate calendar, delete that calendar.

Will importing the same sheet twice create duplicates? With the CSV import, yes. Calendar Import for Google Sheets skips rows it already added.

Does it send invitations? The CSV import does not import guests, and our add-on never uses a guests column, so no invitation emails are sent.

title: How to Translate a Google Slides Presentation Without Breaking the Formatting
ex: Google Slides has no translate command. Three ways to translate a deck: copy and paste, translating the PowerPoint file, or an add-on that keeps colors, bold and links on the translated words.
alt: A Google Slides title in English and the same slide translated into Spanish, with the red word still red
eyealt: Translate Google Slides and keep the formatting
html:
Short answer: Google Slides has no "translate presentation" command in its menus (Google Docs has Tools → Translate document; Slides does not). You can download the deck as PowerPoint, translate the file at translate.google.com (Documents tab) and upload it again, or copy the text slide by slide. Both are slow, and colors, bold words and links often move or disappear. An add-on such as Translate Slides with Formatting (made by us) translates the slides in place, keeps fonts, colors, bold, links and bullets on the right words, and has an Undo button.

Written: November 2026, Google Slides in Chrome.

Which situation are you in?

  • One or two slides: copy and paste with Google Translate (Method 1).
  • A whole deck once, and you do not mind fixing the layout: Method 2.
  • A deck you translate often, or that must keep its formatting: Method 3.

Compare the ways

Method 1: Copy and paste with Google Translate

  1. Select the text in a text box and copy it.
  2. Paste it into translate.google.com, choose the language, and copy the result.
  3. Paste it back over the original text.

Pasting replaces the formatting of the text box, so a word you had in red or bold has to be set again. It is fine for a title slide, tiring for a deck.

Method 2: Translate the PowerPoint file

  1. In Google Slides, choose File → Download → Microsoft PowerPoint (.pptx).
  2. Go to translate.google.com, open the Documents tab, choose the languages and upload the .pptx file (files up to 10 MB).
  3. Download the translated file and upload it to Google Drive. Open it with Google Slides (File → Save as Google Slides if it opens as a PowerPoint file).

You get a translated copy of the whole deck. Check every slide: longer text (English → German or Spanish) can overflow its box, text in images is not translated, and the copy is a separate file, so comments and sharing do not carry over.

Method 3: Translate in place, keeping the formatting (add-on)

Translate Slides with Formatting is an add-on made by us, Daily Picks. It sends each piece of text with its own font, size or color together with a marker, and puts the formatting back around the translated words. In "Our new red car" → "Nuestro nuevo coche rojo", the red word is still red and the bold words are still bold.

  1. Install Translate Slides from the Google Workspace Marketplace.
  2. Open the presentation and choose Extensions → Translate Slides with Formatting → Translate slides.
  3. Choose the language and the slides (this slide, the slides selected on the left, or all).
  4. Press Check to see how many slides, paragraphs and translation calls it will take.
  5. Press Translate. If you do not like the result, press Undo the last translation (twice to confirm).

Longer text is fitted to its box by making that box's font a little smaller (down to 70% at most), and links stay on the translated words. Alignment, spacing and bullets are not touched. Text in images, charts and word art is not changed.

The add-on reads only the presentation you have open and translates with Google's own translation service inside Apps Script; it has no server of its own. Google gives each account a daily number of translations (about 5,000 a day for personal accounts, 20,000 for Google Workspace), so the add-on sends many paragraphs in one call. The free version translates 10 slides per run (press again for the next 10), in every language, with formatting, links, box fitting and Undo, and no watermark or trial period. Paid sets are one-time purchases at $14 each: speaker notes, tables and groups; a glossary of words never translated and fixed translations; and original plus translation side by side, a translated copy, or several languages at once. Everything is $36 one-time, or a subscription that also remembers your corrections. Details are on the Translate Slides product page.

Pitfalls

  • Text overflowing the box: translations into German, French or Spanish are often 20–30% longer. Shrink the font of those boxes, or leave more room in the original.
  • Proper nouns translated: product names and people's names can be translated by mistake. Check them, or keep a list of words that must stay as they are.
  • Speaker notes forgotten: most quick methods translate only the slides. If you present from notes, translate them too.

FAQ

Can Google Slides translate a whole presentation? Not with a built-in command. Google Docs has Translate document; Slides does not. Use the PowerPoint route or an add-on.

Will the formatting stay the same? With copy and paste, no. With the file route, partly. Translate Slides with Formatting keeps fonts, sizes, colors, bold, italics and links on the translated words.

Can I undo a translation? With our add-on, Undo the last translation puts the text and formatting back. File → Version history also keeps the original.

Is there a limit? Google sets a daily translation limit per account. The add-on shows an estimate before you start, and if the limit is reached, what is already translated stays.
